newsitem.title: USA: US stocks end lower as rate pressures halt rebound.
newsitem.headline: US stocks end lower as rate pressures halt rebound.

text.p: The Dow industrials slumped lower on Monday as higher interest rates and a sell-off in tech stocks drained the stock market of its momentum.
The Dow fell 43 points to close unofficially at 6660 after a thinly traded session that saw the New York Stock Exchange register its lowest daily volume this year.

"The volume numbers tell you buyers have really backed away here," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany. "It's not hard to figure out why. It's almost entirely a function of interest rates."
Long-term rates pushed higher on the day, with the yield on the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury rising by four basis points to 7.09 percent, also on extremely thin volume.
The sell-off was far more severe among tech stocks, which dragged the Nasdaq Composite down by 1.5 percent.

As a group, tech stocks enjoyed nowhere near the recovery that blue chips did during their record-setting 312-point rally last week and today's decline actually wiped out Nasdaq's entire gain for the week.

"The tech stocks participated in the rally last week for about 15 minutes," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "And this market is in a near-term downtrend regardless of last week's rally."
Networking shares were among the hardest-hit in the tech sector, with Cisco Systems Inc down 1-1/16 to 47-5/16, 3Com Corp down 2-7/8 to 26-3/8 and Ascend Communications Inc off two to 38-1/4.
Financial stocks were also broadly lower, with Chase Manhattan Corp down two to 85-1/2 and J.P. Morgan & Co Inc shedding 1-1/2 to 95-3/8.
With interest rates again thust into center stage, analysts said stocks could find themselves back on shaky footing if evidence favors further Federal Reserve tightening.
Some saw evidence of jitters about just such a possibility this afternoon, as comments by Fed vice chairman Alice Rivlin during an afternoon speech were made their way to the market.

During her speech, Rivlin referred to "the possible overheating of the economy" as the major threat to the U.S. economy at this time. Analysts were divided on the direct impact of Rivlin's comments, but there was no disagreement on what the impact of a rising interest rate climate would bring.

"Any sustainable advance will depend on the market's estimation as to whether the Fed is out of the picture," said Arun Kumar, strategist at Lehman Brothers. "It looks like the market is looking for 50 basis points more of tightening."

Shares in oil companies were among the few to largely shrug off the weak tone in the market as giants Amoco Corp, Amerada Hess Corp and Exxon Corp all reported earnings that beat Wall Street estimates.
Hess shares rose 3/8 to 49-1/8 and Amoco gained 5/8 to 82. Exxon shares shed 1/8, however, finishing at 53-3/8.

In individual issues, AutoImmune Inc plunged 9-7/16 or 69 percent to 4-5/16 after the company announced a Phase III trial showed no difference in patient response to its multiple sclerosis drug Myloral and a placebo.

APAC TeleServices Inc slid 10-3/8 to 11-1/8 after the company reported lower than expected first quarter earnings. APAC, a marketing services company, also said its year results would be hurt by high costs related to a major contract with United Parcel Service of America Inc.
The S&P 500 index fell 5.97 points to 760.37.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 18.62 points to 1203.95.
((-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730))
